title: Degradation of aerospace wire insulation
summary: Characterized how aerospace wire insulation degrades under heat and vacuum, and built the testing procedure that made the data readable outside the materials group.
problem: Wire insulation on aerospace systems ages in ways that single-number datasheet values don't capture, and the resulting data was hard for non-materials engineers to act on.
approach: Ran TGA, ASTM E595 outgassing, vacuum-oven exposure, FTIR, and Raman across the material set; resolved fiberglass, PTFE, and PVA binder chemistries; then wrote a standardized testing and documentation procedure and the SOPs behind it.
outcome: Results became usable by non-materials audiences, and the characterization work fed directly into the trade study and failure assessment that followed.

log.note: SOPs for TGA, outgassing, and specimen photography finalized.
Binder chemistries resolved across the fiberglass and PTFE set.

title: Color analysis of polymers by machine learning
summary: Extended an existing polymer color-analysis approach to complex materials under extreme heat, with new models reaching 15% higher accuracy. First-author manuscript.
problem: Color change is a cheap, fast proxy for thermal degradation, but prior models only handled simple systems and broke down on complex materials at high temperature.
approach: Built and trained new models against characterization data from extreme-heat exposure, then validated against instrumented measurements.
outcome: 15% accuracy improvement over the prior approach. Manuscript in NASA review, headed to a peer-reviewed journal.

log.note: New model hit 15% accuracy gain over baseline.

title: Polymer trade study and thruster failure assessment
summary: Ranked alternative polymers by cost, manufacturability, and outgassing, and delivered a materials failure assessment on thruster structural integrity that changed the project's scope.
problem: Material selection was being made without a common basis for comparing cost against space-environment performance, and a structural integrity question on the thruster had no empirical answer.
approach: Built a trade study across candidate polymers, coordinated external testing and manufacturer communication on chemistry and qualification methods, and assembled the failure assessment from the characterization data.
outcome: Presented to NASA and industry-partner engineers. The data drove a change in project scope and launched a follow-on effort that I now lead.

log.note: Scope change approved. Follow-on effort started.

title: Ground penetrating radar payload, HS-3
org: Husky Satellite Lab · University of Washington
summary: Leading design of the GPR payload for HS-3, a mission to detect and map habitable lava tubes beneath the lunar surface.
problem: Lunar lava tubes are a candidate for habitation, but mapping them requires a radar payload that fits a student-built satellite's mass, power, and survivability budget.
approach: Currently in design. Working the antenna and payload architecture against the mission's constraints, with attention to how the materials hold up through launch and the lunar thermal cycle.
outcome: In design. Hardware and test results will be posted as the build progresses.

log.note: Design phase. Notebook pages up, hardware to follow.
Took over as lead GPR engineer.

title: CFRP wing spoiler quality recovery
summary: Led a team of five through root-cause analysis and NDT of manufacturing defects in carbon fiber wing spoilers, and set the acceptance criteria that came out of it.
problem: Manufacturing defects were appearing in CFRP wing spoilers without a clear root cause or an agreed standard for what counted as acceptable.
approach: Ran root-cause analysis and non-destructive testing across the affected parts, then worked the findings into acceptance criteria the team could defend.
outcome: Criteria developed and results presented directly to Boeing engineers.
